He offers two explanations, and both are a trap.
Option one: China's leader abandoned his "East rising, West declining" worldview because of a hug. Read that back to him. He has just described a head of state who rewrites grand strategy at the bottom of an airplane stair — and, in the same sentence, an America that one embrace can move. He arrived to belittle Beijing and drafted an insult to Washington without noticing. Neither portrait flatters anyone.
Option two: the Chinese economy is "weaker than it looks." Weaker by how much? By what measure? He never says, and nothing could ever prove him wrong, because he alone keeps the definition of what it looks like. That is not analysis; it is a talisman. One sentence, twenty-five years, and not once has it carried a piece of information. Meanwhile the country he writes off hosted this summit, on its own soil, at its own airport, with a goods trade surplus past a trillion dollars.
The door he deleted is the obvious one: a state that no longer needs to prove its strength can simply be glad to see its guest.
Then the mistranslation — the part that actually matters. "New era" names a stage of China's own development; it is a sentence about what China intends to do at home. He did not translate it, he replaced it: "what China will do" became "who will rule." It has to come out wrong. Translated faithfully, the phrase is untelevisable, and there is no threat left to sell.
Then the chair, and the strange question of whose anger it is. The guest rode through a Chinese city with his curtains open and flew home with agreements; nobody in the White House complained. Mr. Chang's claim is not that America was insulted — it is that he knows better than the president of the United States whether the president was insulted. One man was wounded by that seat, and he is in a studio.
He says someone ought to call it out. Someone already did, twice this year, in his own government's own words: "too negative," "not true."

🗞️ The line for onchain trading is drawn: same rules as everyone else.

CFTC (Commodity Futures Trading Commission) @CFTC Chair Michael Selig told Hyperliquid @HyperliquidX and its rivals that running on a blockchain buys no exemption — to offer perpetual futures to US retail traders, a venue either registers as an exchange or partners with one that already is.

"We're not going to treat you differently and say because it's onchain, you have a different set of requirements," Selig said on Thursday at the Capitol Crypto Forum in Washington. "You're going to have to come in and partner with an exchange or obtain your own exchange."

Selig pointed to a Nov 16 agency statement: the Commodity Exchange Act sets the principles for exchanges without prescribing any particular technology, and said venues must still clear the same bars on asset segregation, anti-money-laundering controls, market surveillance, and risk management.

Backpack @Backpack is the proof: all three licences — clearinghouse Nov 13, exchange Nov 16, futures-broker registration Nov 18.

Who's already moving:
- Kraken's parent Payward announced in September that Bitnomial, its CFTC-regulated exchange, would deploy markets on Hyperliquid's infrastructure — all subject to approval.
- Hyperliquid Strategies disclosed on Nov 5 that subsidiary HypeStrat Markets applied in August to register as a futures broker, which would let it carry US client accounts.

Hong Kong's regulator added Hyperliquid to its suspicious-platforms list on Nov 18, saying it was unlicensed and suspected of marketing to local investors. In May, CME Group @CMEGroup and Intercontinental Exchange called for an investigation into possible market manipulation and sanctions violations. Neither regulator has publicly taken enforcement action.

In Plain English
Onchain is a technology choice, not a regulatory category. The CFTC is offering a door, register or partner, and warning the alternative is the business moving offshore. "These things are going to happen. It's a question of where they happen," Selig said. "If we don't allow them here, they're just going to go offshore."

Why This Is Bullish
A clear rule beats a grey one. The biggest onchain perps venue now has a named route to US traders — through licences, not loopholes. That is how a market graduates from offshore to onshore.

My Take
Selig is not anti-crypto; he is anti-exception. "That may upset some on the crypto side that want everything to be completely unregulated, but that's not fair to the incumbents who have had to comply with all these rules." The question now is speed: Backpack did it in a week.

Which arrives first for US traders — a regulated Hyperliquid market, or a new fight over who regulates perps?

Fine Print
- Hyperliquid itself remains unavailable to US customers. Every proposed route above is subject to approval — none is live yet.
- Congress's market-structure bill failed 49-50 in the Senate in September; the two agencies are writing their own crypto rules meanwhile.

THE SOVEREIGNTY TRAP: BREXIT, SERBIA AND THE POLITICS OF FOREIGN INFLUENCE

Ten years after Britain voted to leave the European Union, the country is negotiating its way back towards Brussels. Meanwhile, Serbia faces its own sovereignty test as the Student List prepares to translate political victory into governing power. The question facing both countries is ultimately the same: who decides a nation's future?

On June 23, 2016, the British electorate delivered a political shock that reverberated across Europe and challenged the foundations of the European Union. Britain voted to leave.

The message was unmistakable. Millions of voters wanted greater control over their country's borders, laws, economy and political destiny. They believed decisions affecting Britain should be made in Britain, by representatives accountable to British voters.

Ten years later, the political establishment is confronting an uncomfortable reality. Britain is once again negotiating closer relations with Brussels.

On November 20, 2026, Prime Minister Andy Burnham and European Union leaders reached agreements covering agricultural trade, emissions trading and youth mobility. The arrangements are intended to remove barriers, reduce costs and rebuild a relationship that has been strained since Brexit.

Yet the agreements come with an important qualification: closer access to European markets requires Britain to align with certain European regulatory standards, without regaining an equivalent voice in making those rules.

Britain has discovered something that political campaigns rarely acknowledge: leaving a political institution does not mean escaping economic interdependence.

But the significance of this moment extends well beyond the United Kingdom.

Because another European country is facing a remarkably similar question, albeit from a very different starting point.

That country is Serbia.

BRITAIN: THE COST OF TAKING BACK CONTROL

Brexit was never simply a disagreement about customs arrangements or agricultural regulations. It was a fundamental argument about sovereignty.

Supporters believed Britain had surrendered too much political authority to European institutions. Opponents warned that leaving the world's largest single market would introduce economic friction, undermine investment and diminish Britain's international influence.

Both sides made arguments that deserved serious consideration.

What followed demonstrated the difficulty of translating political independence into economic prosperity.

British exporters faced additional administrative requirements. Businesses operating across European supply chains encountered new barriers. The promised economic opportunities of independent trade policy proved more complicated than campaign rhetoric suggested.

Now, Burnham's government is attempting to repair some of that damage.

But the question remains: if Britain must increasingly align its regulations with Brussels to secure economic advantages, what exactly does its independent status deliver?

That does not mean Brexit was necessarily wrong, nor does it mean returning to the EU would automatically solve Britain's economic problems.

It means sovereignty must be measured against actual economic and political outcomes, not simply the language used to sell it.

SERBIA: A DIFFERENT MODEL OF POLITICAL INDEPENDENCE

Serbia has approached the European question from a fundamentally different position.

Unlike Britain, Serbia has never been an EU member. It remains a candidate country, negotiating the terms of closer integration while maintaining relationships with other major international powers.

Under Aleksandar Vučić, Belgrade pursued a foreign policy that sought to preserve strategic flexibility.

Serbia maintained its European membership ambitions while expanding economic cooperation with China, retaining historical and political relationships with Russia, engaging Washington and developing relations with Israel.

This approach was not without controversy.

Brussels repeatedly expressed frustration with Serbia's refusal to align fully with European foreign policy, particularly regarding sanctions against Russia. Washington maintained its own expectations concerning regional security, Kosovo and Serbia's broader strategic orientation.

Yet the underlying calculation was straightforward: Serbia's national interests could not be reduced to choosing one geopolitical camp.

For a country with Serbia's history, geographical position, economic circumstances and unresolved territorial questions, maintaining multiple international relationships has obvious strategic considerations.

Vučić's approach was not without compromises, contradictions or domestic criticism. But it placed the question of Serbia's room for manoeuvre at the centre of its foreign policy.

The important distinction is that maintaining relationships with competing powers is not the same as surrendering national decision-making to any one of them.

THE STUDENT LIST: FROM PROTEST MOVEMENT TO POLITICAL RESPONSIBILITY

This is where Serbia's political transformation becomes particularly significant.

The Student List's October 25 electoral victory, securing approximately 140 seats in the 250-member National Assembly, ended 14 years of Serbian Progressive Party dominance.

The movement emerged from two years of student-led protests and built its political appeal around anti-corruption, institutional reform and demands for accountability.

Its victory was a significant democratic development.

But winning an election and governing a country are two very different responsibilities.

During the protests, the movement could operate around broad principles and a common opposition to the existing political establishment.

Government requires something considerably more demanding: an identifiable leadership, a coherent economic programme, clear foreign policy priorities and accountability for decisions.

And this is where some of the most important questions remain.

What is the Student List's long-term economic strategy?

How will it balance European integration with Serbia's relationships with China and Russia?

What will its approach be towards Washington, NATO, Kosovo and Israel?

How will it protect Serbia's economic interests while negotiating with international institutions that have their own political and strategic priorities?

These are not peripheral questions. They concern the fundamental direction of the Serbian state.

The movement has publicly indicated that it does not support imposing sanctions on Russia and maintains positions on military neutrality and Kosovo that broadly preserve existing Serbian policy. Those positions deserve to be examined alongside its other commitments, rather than assuming that a change of government automatically means a complete geopolitical realignment.

But the larger concern remains: what happens when a movement that built its political identity around challenging existing institutions must now negotiate with the international actors that have their own expectations of Serbia?

BRUSSELS AND WASHINGTON: THE QUESTION OF INFLUENCE

European governments welcomed the Student List's victory, with European Commissioner for Enlargement Marta Kos suggesting that the result could create an opportunity to advance Serbia's European integration.

That reaction is understandable. Brussels has a direct institutional interest in Serbia's political direction.

Washington has its own strategic interests in the Balkans. So do Moscow and Beijing.

None of these powers approaches Serbia without national interests of its own.

Foreign governments routinely use diplomacy, investment, development assistance, political engagement and institutional partnerships to influence the direction of countries they consider strategically important.

That is not unique to Serbia. It is how international politics operates.

But there is a distinction between international cooperation and political dependency.

The question is not whether Serbia should cooperate with Brussels or Washington. It should engage constructively with both.

The question is whether its future political leadership can negotiate those relationships independently, or whether the expectations of external partners will increasingly determine domestic priorities.

The Student List must answer that question through its decisions, appointments, policies and governing record.

Political independence cannot be established simply by declaring it.

Nor can foreign control be established merely by pointing to diplomatic support or political congratulations. Evidence matters.

But transparency matters equally.

Serbian voters have a legitimate interest in knowing who influences the country's political direction, how political and financial relationships operate, and whether the people making decisions in Belgrade are accountable first and foremost to the Serbian electorate.

THE ECONOMIC DIMENSION: SOVEREIGNTY WITHOUT PROSPERITY IS AN EMPTY PROMISE

There is another lesson Britain offers Serbia.

Political sovereignty and economic prosperity are related, but they are not interchangeable.

Britain discovered that leaving the European Union did not eliminate its dependence on European markets. Serbia, in turn, cannot build a prosperous economy by isolating itself from European capital, international trade or global investment.

Serbia needs investment, technology transfer, infrastructure, competitive industries, energy security and access to international markets.

Its relationships with China, Russia, the European Union and the United States all have economic implications.

The challenge is to negotiate arrangements that produce measurable benefits for Serbian businesses, workers and taxpayers.

European integration should not be treated as an ideological destination independent of economic outcomes. Nor should cooperation with China or Russia be treated as an automatic guarantee of economic advantage.

Every partnership should be evaluated on its terms.

What does Serbia receive? What does it contribute? What obligations does it accept? What strategic flexibility does it retain?

These are the questions a serious government must answer.

And they are precisely the questions that political movements often avoid while campaigning.

THE BIGGER EUROPEAN QUESTION

The Brexit debate and Serbia's political transition reveal a common challenge facing European democracies.

Countries increasingly operate in a world where economic integration, security arrangements, technology, energy and international capital connect national interests across borders.

No serious government can pretend that it operates in isolation.

But neither should economic interdependence automatically become an argument for political subordination.

Britain voted to leave the EU and is now negotiating closer cooperation because economic realities have complicated its original political ambitions.

Serbia has remained outside the EU while attempting to maintain relationships with competing powers. Its new political leadership must now demonstrate whether it can preserve that strategic flexibility while pursuing economic development and institutional reform.

These are different political journeys, but they lead to the same fundamental question.

How does a country cooperate with powerful international institutions without allowing those institutions to determine its domestic political priorities?

The answer requires something more substantial than campaign slogans, diplomatic photographs or declarations of national independence.

It requires transparent institutions, competent leadership, economic discipline and political accountability.

THE FINAL TEST: WHO DOES THE GOVERNMENT ANSWER TO?

The British electorate made its decision in 2016. Ten years later, the country is reconsidering the practical consequences of that decision.

Serbia's electorate has now made a different decision, bringing the Student List to the threshold of government and ending an era of political dominance.

Both countries face a test that extends beyond their immediate political circumstances.

Britain must explain what closer integration with Brussels means for the sovereignty its electorate once demanded.

Serbia's incoming leadership must explain how it intends to balance European ambitions, American expectations, Russian relationships and Chinese investment while protecting the country's national interests.

The Student List cannot indefinitely rely on the political legitimacy it acquired through protest. Its legitimacy will increasingly depend on the decisions it makes in government.

If it promises institutional independence, it must demonstrate it.

If it promises economic reform, it must deliver it.

If it promises to defend Serbia's sovereignty, it must explain precisely how it intends to do so.

And if foreign governments welcome its arrival, that is not itself evidence of improper influence. But it makes transparency about diplomatic, financial and political relationships even more important.

There is a fundamental difference between a government that chooses international partnerships because they benefit its citizens and one that allows external expectations to dictate its priorities.

Sovereignty is not about refusing to deal with Brussels, Washington, Moscow or Beijing. It is about having the political independence to deal with all of them without forgetting who elected you.

Britain's Brexit experience demonstrates the economic consequences of political decisions. Serbia's transition will demonstrate whether a new political generation understands the responsibilities that come with national sovereignty.

Ultimately, the measure of any government is not how warmly it is received in foreign capitals.

It is whether the people who elected it remain the first priority when the difficult decisions begin.

WHAT THEY ARE SAYING: Send the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act to President Trump’s Desk

FOR IMMEDIATE RELEASE

"Last night, landmark permitting reform legislation passed the Senate. It's one of the biggest things that you will see. It's a big deal… It’s projected to put at least $1,300 a year back in the pockets of hardworking Americans.” – President Donald J. Trump

President Donald J. Trump is committed to fixing America’s broken permitting system standing behind (BAAJA), legislation that will modernize federal environmental reviews and permitting while delivering cheaper energy, high-paying jobs, and economic growth across the United States.

Last night, the Senate advanced landmark permitting reform legislation, and now the House has the opportunity to finish the job and send the bill to President Trump’s desk to lock in generations of affordability and energy dominance for the American people.

Here’s what they’re saying about the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act:

American Exploration & Production Council CEO Anne Bradbury: “AXPC applauds the Senate for taking decisive bipartisan action to remove longstanding barriers to American energy and infrastructure development. BAAJA offers a generational opportunity to cut through permitting delays and lower costs across America without compromising critical environmental protections. With meaningful relief for American families within reach, we respectfully urge the House to send BAAJA to the President’s desk before the end of the year.”

American Chemistry Council: “Yesterday’s vote represents an important step toward addressing longstanding permitting challenges that have delayed projects, increased costs, and hindered economic growth. As demand for energy, advanced manufacturing, and critical infrastructure continues to grow, the United States needs a permitting system capable of supporting investment and development at the speed required to compete globally.

“The future of American manufacturing, infrastructure, and energy development depends on our nation's ability to build. Enactment of this legislation would help ensure the United States remains the best place in the world to invest, manufacture, and innovate “

American Petroleum Institute President and CEO Mike Sommers: “Today’s bipartisan Senate vote marks a major breakthrough on historic permitting reforms that would deliver more affordable energy for consumers, cut costly delays, and build much-needed critical infrastructure. We thank Senators Capito, Lee, Whitehouse and Heinrich for advancing long-overdue reforms.”

Association of American Railroads CEO and President Ian Jefferies: “Senate passage of the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act is an encouraging step toward a permitting process that works better for communities and the projects they depend on. Freight railroads make long-term investments in the network that connects businesses, farms, ports, and consumers. When reviews take years, needed improvements can be delayed. This bipartisan legislation can help make project reviews timelier and more predictable while preserving important environmental protections.”

Business Roundtable CEO Joshua Bolten: “Business Roundtable applauds the Senate for passing the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act of 2026. The strong bipartisan vote marks an important step toward enacting comprehensive permitting reforms that would help lower costs for American families and businesses.

“By modernizing the federal permitting system, this legislation would make it easier to build critical energy projects, roads, ports and other much-needed infrastructure. The benefits would flow to Americans in the form of lower utility bills, new good-paying jobs and more private-sector investment in communities across the country. We urge the House to finish the job and swiftly pass this measure.”

Interstate Natural Gas Association of America President and CEO Amy Andryszak: “Tonight’s Senate vote marks a pivotal step toward modernizing America’s permitting process and ensuring affordable energy for American consumers. Enshrining improvements to the Clean Water Act, the National Environmental Policy Act (NEPA), judicial reviews, and permit certainty in statute will help accelerate the buildout of the critical energy infrastructure needed to meet growing demand and ensure a reliable, affordable energy future.

“We applaud Senators for reaching bipartisan consensus and urge the U.S. House of Representatives to act quickly to send this legislation to the President’s desk. The House must pass this legislation without further delay to help meet America’s energy needs and address rising energy costs.”

Laborers International Union of North America President Brent Booker: “For more than a decade, endless permitting delays have stalled critical infrastructure projects that put our members to work across the country. Every month a project sits on the shelf, LIUNA members go without paychecks. This bill ends the runaround. It sets clear timelines and holds the process accountable, so projects get decided and built. Congress has spent years talking about the need to fix our broken permitting process. Now it has a real opportunity to do something about it. The cost of inaction is too high: lost jobs, lost investment, and lost opportunities for working Americans. We cannot afford to let another Congress come and go while critical projects remain stalled and working families pay the price.”

National Association of Home Builders: “With so many families priced out of the market, the House must pass this bill without delay. BAAJA will make federal permits faster and less costly for builders and developers, lowering land development costs and making lots more affordable. It also helps multifamily developers by ensuring that the use of federal grants and loans does not automatically trigger a National Environmental Policy Act (NEPA) review. For projects that still need a NEPA review, the bill sets enforceable deadlines for agencies to complete it.”

National Electrical Manufacturers Association President and CEO Debra Phillips: “America’s electricity needs are growing rapidly, and this legislation will help us build the infrastructure to meet them. It speeds up transmission projects, encourages grid-enhancing advanced transmission technologies, and gives investors more certainty, which means more reliable, affordable power for consumers. That will help America build the energy system our future demands, and move past an outdated permitting system that has been tangled in red tape for too long. We commend the bipartisan leadership that made this progress possible and urge the House to finish the job.”

National Mining Association President and CEO Rich Nolan: “We’re grateful to the Senate for coming together to move legislation that will help transform American potential into American production, and for the leadership of Senators Capito, Whitehouse, Lee and Heinrich, who deserve great credit for their tireless work to advance the bill. True economic and national security comes with a United States that can build things again, using domestic materials and domestic fuels, and decisively confront China’s supply chain dominance. It’s now up to the House to say American prosperity and competitiveness matter, ensure that made in America can also be mined in America, and pass this legislation.”

National Rural Electric Cooperative Association CEO Jim Matheson: “This legislation will dramatically improve the federal permitting system, making it more manageable and predictable for electric co-ops as they work to keep the lights on at a cost families and businesses can afford. Today’s environmental review processes can take years, delaying critical energy projects and increasing costs that ultimately fall on consumers. The bill will streamline reviews and reduce litigation delays, while leaving important environmental protections in place.”

U.S. Oil and Gas Association President Tim Stewart: "BAAJA brought together the broadest and most diverse coalition of working interests that Washington has seen in decades who worked to pass a good piece of legislation that will let us build things in America again.

“It will ensure greater abundance and affordability for the next generation and we are proud to be a part of it.”

Western Energy Alliance: “We have a generational choice in front of us. We must decide if we’re going to be builders or not. If we’re going to meet our nation’s energy needs, or not. text:
Let us separate fact from fiction when it comes to Thomas Jefferson and Alexander Hamilton. In the earliest days of the United States, while the young nation was still fragile and uncertain of its survival, two brilliant men sat across from each other at President George Washington's cabinet table.
 
Behind closed doors, Thomas Jefferson, serving as Secretary of State, and Alexander Hamilton, serving as Secretary of the Treasury, waged a quiet war over what kind of country America would actually become. The stakes could not have been higher, because the winning vision would decide whether power belonged to ordinary people or to a select few at the top.
 
At first, their disagreements seemed like simple arguments over policy, but beneath the surface lay a deep divide over who could be trusted with freedom. Jefferson placed his faith in everyday citizens, family farmers, and local communities to govern themselves. He believed that when people own their own land and manage their own affairs, they stay independent and free from the control of powerful elites.
 
Hamilton and his fellow federalists saw things very differently. They quietly harbored deep doubts about ordinary voters, believing that a strong central government needed to be tied closely to a wealthy ruling class. In fact, the federalists openly attacked Jefferson as a man of the people, using it as an insult and branding him a dangerous demagogue because they genuinely believed that trusting everyday citizens would lead to mob rule and chaos.
 
Just how far apart their minds truly were came to light during a private dinner party hosted by Jefferson in 1791. Hanging on the dining room wall were portraits of three men Jefferson considered the greatest figures in human history: Francis Bacon, Isaac Newton, and John Locke. Each of those three thinkers had changed the world by advancing science, reason, and individual liberty.
 
During a lull in the evening, Hamilton noticed the portraits and asked who they were. Jefferson explained why he admired them so deeply, then waited for Hamilton's reaction. According to Jefferson's later account of the evening, Hamilton paused and gave a chilling answer, stating that the greatest man who ever lived was Julius Caesar, the Roman general who marched his army into Rome and ruled as an absolute dictator.
 
That admiration for strong, top-down rule was not just a passing dinner-table remark. Four years earlier, in the summer of 1787, delegates from across the states had gathered in Philadelphia for the Constitutional Convention to design a new government for the United States. On June 18 of that year, Hamilton stood on the convention floor and delivered a massive, six-hour speech laying out his ideal system.
 
According to James Madison's detailed notes from the convention, Hamilton openly praised the British monarchy as the best government in the world. He argued that every society naturally divides into two groups, the wealthy few and the common many, and claimed that ordinary citizens were too turbulent and changing to be trusted with real power. To solve this, Hamilton proposed that the American president and senators should serve for life, much like the British king and House of Lords, so the rich and well-born could hold a permanent share of power to keep the common people in check.
 
Although the other delegates rejected lifetime rulers, that same distrust of everyday citizens shaped everything Hamilton built once he became Secretary of the Treasury. Soon after taking office, Hamilton pushed through a massive national bank modeled on the British system, along with an excise tax on whiskey passed in 1791 to pay off Revolutionary War debts.
 
Under Hamilton's financial system, wealthy city speculators who had bought up war bonds from desperate soldiers for pennies on the dollar were paid back at full value. Meanwhile, struggling frontier farmers in western Pennsylvania were hit with a tax that punished small producers far harder than large eastern distillers. Because cash was scarce on the frontier, farmers turned their surplus grain into whiskey so they could transport it over the mountains and use it as money to trade for basic supplies. Hamilton's law demanded they pay the tax in hard cash, and anyone accused of falling behind faced trial in a federal court 300 miles away in Philadelphia.
 
By 1794, frustration boiled over into what became known as the Whiskey Rebellion, and blood was soon spilled. Angry farmers tarred and feathered tax collectors, and in July 1794, around 500 armed men surrounded the home of regional tax inspector John Neville. During the gunfight that followed, rebel leader James McFarlane, a respected Revolutionary War veteran, was shot and killed after stepping out during what he believed was a ceasefire, along with a few other protesters and a soldier defending the house.
 
Soon after, nearly 7,000 protesters gathered near Pittsburgh. Instead of fixing the unfair tax, Hamilton urged the use of overwhelming military force to crush the resistance. In the fall of 1794, nearly 13,000 militia troops were mobilized and marched into western Pennsylvania, with Hamilton riding alongside the army to supervise the crackdown.
 
To many Americans who had just fought for independence, the sight of an armed force marching into communities to enforce an unpopular tax and haul citizens to distant courts felt painfully reminiscent of the British crown they had only recently overthrown. By the time the soldiers arrived, the protesters had already scattered without a battle, yet troops occupied the region, arrested around 150 men, and accidentally killed two local civilians during the occupation.
 
As Hamilton's system took hold, Jefferson sounded the alarm, warning that the government was using heavy taxes and armed force to enrich the few at the expense of the many. Jefferson insisted that federal officials only held the powers clearly written in the Constitution, and nowhere did that document allow Congress to create a giant banking monopoly. As a republican (written with a lowercase r, as people of that era used the word for their movement, completely separate from the modern-day Republican Party), Jefferson fought to keep taxes low, pay off the national debt instead of using permanent debt to bind wealthy bondholders to the state, and protect the rights of individual citizens and states from distant rulers.
 
The true test of both men's ideas finally arrived when Jefferson became president in 1801, giving him the chance to put his principles into action. He quickly abolished all federal internal taxes, including the hated whiskey tax, relying instead on customs duties on foreign imports so federal tax collectors no longer knocked on the doors of ordinary families.
 
At the same time, Jefferson slashed unnecessary government spending, cut the national debt by more than 31 percent during his eight years in office, and doubled the size of the country through the Louisiana Purchase so generations of American families could own their own farms.
 
Defenders of Hamilton often push back against this picture by pointing out that both men were wealthy elites, that Hamilton helped ratify the Constitution through the Federalist Papers, and that he even backed Jefferson over Aaron Burr in 1800 because he feared Burr was a dangerous opportunist. They also argue that Hamilton's 1787 convention speech was only a theoretical sketch, and that his financial system deserves credit for establishing strong public credit, creating a reliable money supply, and helping the young nation borrow money abroad to grow its economy.
 
Yet even when we credit Hamilton with strengthening public borrowing, Jefferson's presidency proved that America did not need permanent debt, internal taxes, or a wealthy banking elite to prosper and maintain strong credit. Under Jefferson, the United States paid down its debts ahead of schedule, kept its international credit rock solid, and funded the largest peaceful land expansion in American history without taxing a single farmer's whiskey or wages. Hamilton's approach always asked ordinary people to shoulder taxes and debt so wealth and credit could flow down from the top, whereas Jefferson proved that a nation thrives best when citizens keep what they earn and build prosperity from the ground up.
 
Furthermore, Jefferson respected strict constitutional boundaries even when facing the biggest decision of his presidency. When Jefferson wondered whether a constitutional amendment was needed to buy Louisiana, he did not simply grab power on his own. Instead, he consulted with his cabinet and with Secretary of State James Madison, the Father of the Constitution himself, who confirmed that the treaty power already written in the Constitution allowed the purchase, before submitting the treaty to the Senate for approval so working families could gain millions of acres of land.
 
When that contrast is placed alongside the Sedition Act of 1798, which Hamilton's federalist allies used to fine and imprison republican newspaper editors, printers, and critics simply for speaking out against the government, the real divide of the 1790s comes into sharp focus. One of the most famous targets was Matthew Lyon, an Irish-born Revolutionary War veteran and sitting Congressman from Vermont who was sentenced to four months in a freezing jail cell and fined $1000, a staggering sum equal to more than $27,000 today, for publishing a letter criticizing President John Adams, yet still won re-election to Congress from behind bars. 

As soon as Jefferson took office, he pardoned every single person convicted under that unconstitutional law, supported refunding their fines, and never once used federal law to prosecute a newspaper editor despite facing vicious personal attacks in the press throughout his entire presidency.
 
When the record is laid side by side, the choice between a vision built around wealthy bondholders, permanent debt, and top-down control versus a vision built around free speech, low taxes, and trust in everyday citizens speaks for itself. What the federalists meant as an insult was actually Jefferson's greatest strength. Unlike those who feared the public and sought permanent shields for the wealthy elite, Jefferson truly was the man of the people, and he offered the stronger foundation for a free nation.

Playa Bagdad, Mexico: more than 1,500 pieces of debris collected since Tuesday, 20 km south of Starbase. Conibio Global, a local conservation group, says it's  Booster 42's internal lining.

The Starship Flight 15 booster self-destructed about 7 minutes after launch on Friday the 13th, a planned sequence initiated when it hit the water. Four days later, plastic, tape, rubber and aluminum started washing up near Matamoros. 

Mexico's environmental agency Profepa says SpaceX must take responsibility. SpaceX says its partners found very little debris and it isn't clear any of it is theirs, but offered to help.

Cleanup crews from Profepa, Mexico's Navy and Tamaulipas are still walking the beach with no end date.

On Starship’s 15th flight last week, the Super Heavy booster correctly performed a safe abort when returning for a catch and ended its mission with a splashdown in the water off the coast of Starbase. Following splashdown, SpaceX recovery teams were immediately onsite to safe the area while our Environmental Health and Safety team worked to ensure any debris that washes onshore was recovered → https://t.co/ALNcWBQinC

When we received reports of potential debris in Mexican territory, we immediately mobilized to send specialists to aid in identification and lead any cleanup work required, just as we did on Boca Chica Beach near Starbase. We continue to stay in contact with the Mexican government and are on standby to send support if authorities in Mexico tell us it is actually needed. Partners on the ground relayed that theyhave found very little debris in their sweeps of the beach, and the small amount they have found are not clearly from SpaceX operations.

The majority of the social media posts online claiming widespread debris and damage are either outright fabrications or intentionally misleading. As repeatedly stated, independent tests conducted on materials inside Starship and the Super Heavy booster, including toxicity analyses, confirm they pose no chemical, biological, or toxicological risks.

Starship is designed to be fully reusable, with future missions planning to return all hardware back to the launch site for catch and reuse. SpaceX is the only one, whether company or country, that has demonstrated this capability is now possible.

A gunman was spotted on a rooftop with a clear line of sight to Donald Trump. Minutes later, the former president was shot in the head, and an American was dead. How was someone able to get that close to assassinating a former president?

What if July 13, 2024, was Trump's JFK moment where agencies or institutions arranged the hit to stop an uncooperative president? 

I've wondered whether the assassination attempt changed Trump's understanding of the people and institutions surrounding the presidency. Before Butler, he had repeatedly campaigned against new wars, funding foreign countries and emphasized diplomacy. Could coming within inches of death have changed how he approached those decisions?

The former Navy SEAL Sniper sees it differently. He believes the shooter acted alone and that the security failure came down to hesitation, poor judgment, and a lack of trust in leadership.

Sam offers a theory about what went wrong with the Secret Service during the assassination attempt in Butler, Pennsylvania. And his explanation raises some serious questions about the people responsible for protecting our country's leaders.

He believes the problem may have been a lack of confidence in leadership. Agents who spotted a potential threat might have hesitated to act because they feared the consequences of making the wrong decision.

“If I pull this trigger, my boss doesn't have my back.”

His theory is that nobody wanted to take responsibility until the threat was undeniable. By then, Trump had already been shot.

Two different explanations, but both lead to the same question.

How does a man with a rifle get into position to shoot a former president, and who is ultimately held accountable when the people assigned to protect him fail?

text:
Jake Tapper (@jaketapper) the Negro Nightwatchman Newt Lee Evidence Deserves an Answer

Jake Tapper, your description of the Leo Frank controversy elucidation by Kingsley Wilson @KingsleyCortes  as “ahistorical antisemitic garbage” requires a closer examination of the evidence concerning Newt Lee. 

The public accusation that Leo Max Frank attempted to direct suspicion toward his graveyard shift security guard was discussed during the original investigation, developed through testimony, and argued by the prosecution at Frank’s 1913 trial. Its historical basis can be examined in the Atlanta Constitution, Atlanta Georgian, Atlanta Journal, and the trial’s Brief of Evidence (Tapper, 1; AG, 22; AJ, 23; AC, 24). I publish those newspapers on my website at https://t.co/MNvBytB3CS 

Kingsley Wilson’s statement that Frank “tried to frame a Black man” did not name that man. This account concerns Newt Lee specifically. It examines the prosecution’s argument that Frank’s changing description of Lee’s time slip, the request to search Frank’s residence, the suggestion that Lee had time to travel home, and the discovery of a bloody shirt at Lee’s residence formed a connected effort to redirect the investigation (Sales, 2). There were three pieces of evidence that attempted to Frame Newt Lee: a forged time slip, a blood soaked shirt planted at Lee's room, and death notes describing Newt Lee.

The Setting: A Black Watchman in Jim Crow Georgia

Newt Lee faced the investigation within a society that formally restricted Negro political participation and enforced racial segregation. Atlanta had experienced a deadly racial riot in 1906, over the rape of four White women. These conditions shaped the world in which a Black factory watchman was questioned about the death of a white girl (Cobb & Inscoe, 3). In 1913 Atlanta it was considered the ultimate crime for a Negro to rape and murder a White girl. This is what made Newt Lee the perfect Patsy for Leo Frank's racist plot to frame him for the Mary Phagan rape-murder, because the emotions would run high against a perceived Black assailant.

Saturday Night and Sunday Morning, April 26–27: Lee’s Duties and Discovery

Lee’s duties at the National Pencil Company included registering his rounds on a watchman’s clock at approximately half-hour intervals. The resulting paper record, variously called a time slip, (tape, or sheet), could therefore be used to test his account of where he had been during the night.

Lee testified that he discovered Mary Phagan’s body in the factory basement early Sunday morning, April 27, 1913, about 3:15 a.m., and summoned the police using the phone in Leo Frank's second floor office. According to the Georgian’s account of his trial testimony, officers “grabbed me and said I did it as soon as I showed them the body.” The man who reported the discovery immediately became a suspect (AG, 4). Two notes found next to the body immediately pointed to Lee as well.

Lee did not claim to have witnessed the killing. His testimony concerned his work, his encounters with Frank, the discovery, and the investigation.

Sunday, April 27: Frank Initially Approved the Record

Reporting Lee’s inquest testimony on April 30, the Georgian quoted him as saying that “on Sunday morning he said I had never lost a punch.” Lee attributed that statement to Frank (AG, 5).

The Georgian also reported that Frank described the record as regular when speaking to its reporter on Sunday afternoon (AG, 6).

The Journal’s April 30 inquest report described Lee maintaining his account under questioning. Lee recalled Frank’s approval: “He said it was all right.” It also placed assistant superintendent N. V. Darley in the examination of the clock record (AJ, 10).

Monday, April 28: Lee Said Frank Changed His Account

In the same April 30 inquest report, the Georgian quoted Lee’s account of the change: “he told me on Monday morning that the clock was not punched right” (AG, 5).

Lee described a changed explanation. The prosecution sought to prove deliberate manipulation through evidence about the paper’s handling, the clock’s operation, the suggested trip home, and the bloody shirt.

Monday, April 28: Herbert Haas Requested a Search of Frank’s Residence

Detective John R. Black later testified that Herbert Haas, one of Frank’s attorneys, requested a search of Frank’s residence and clothing. Black placed the request at approximately 11:30 a.m. on Monday, April 28, 1913, this was two days after the murder. It would have given Leo Frank enough time to wash out any stains in his dirty laundry. 

Reporting Black’s testimony, the Journal described Haas’s insistence that “nothing should be left undone.” This was the newspaper’s account of Black’s explanation of events and communication, not an independently recorded quotation from Haas (AJ, 7).

The Alleged Opportunity: Enough Time for Lee to Go Home and Return

Black’s testimony connected the disputed clock record to a proposed journey by Lee. In the Brief of Evidence, Black attributed to Frank the claim that the irregular record allowed Lee enough time to go home and return. Black also acknowledged uncertainty about whether Frank made the statement before or after the bloody shirt was discovered (BOE, 8).

Tuesday, April 29: Police Found a Bloody Shirt at Lee’s Residence

Black’s account in the Brief of Evidence placed the discovery of a bloody shirt at Lee’s residence on Tuesday morning, April 29, at approximately 9 a.m. He described finding it among clothes in a barrel (BOE, 8).

The shirt gave the disputed time record an additional possible use. If investigators accepted that Lee had sufficient time to travel home, they could interpret the shirt as clothing he had removed after involvement in the killing.

The prosecution later argued that the shirt was planted and the suggested trip home helped make it appear incriminating (AJ, 23; AC, 24).

Wednesday, April 30: The Constitution Raised the Possibility of Planted Evidence

The possibility of a frame-up appeared in the Atlanta press within days of the murder. On April 30, the Constitution asked: “Is the watchman suspect a victim of planted evidence?” (AC, 9).

The same report described three gaps in the clock record: from 9:32 to 10:29 p.m., from 11:04 p.m. to midnight, and from 2 to 3 a.m. Those intervals amount to 57 minutes, 56 minutes, and 60 minutes. Each was roughly twice the expected half-hour interval (AC, 9).

These separate gaps did not establish a continuous three-hour absence or prove that Lee left the building, but everyone wanted to know how the time slip went from being "alright" according to Leo Frank, on Sunday, April 27, 1913, to becoming mispunched four times on Monday, April 28, 1913, according to the factory boss.

Wednesday, April 30: Frank’s Newspaper Interview Added Another Statement

The Journal also published an interview in which Frank expressed surprise at the suggestion that Lee had failed to register regularly. Frank reportedly said: “I don't remember ever having heard of Lee's failing to punch the clock at regular intervals” (AJ, 11).

This was a newspaper interview, not sworn inquest testimony.

If Frank had already identified the irregularities attributed to Lee, why did his interview express unfamiliarity with Lee missing regular registrations? The accounts described different conversations and require comparison.

Thursday, May 8: “Boots” Rogers Challenged the Missing-Punch Account

W. W. “Boots” Rogers, a former policeman and squadcar driver who accompanied officers during the early investigation, became a particularly useful witness because he said he had personally observed the slip.

At the continued inquest on May 8, the Georgian reported Rogers’s statement: “Frank took it into the office and put it on file.” Asked about missing registrations, Rogers answered: “I would have noticed if there were” (AG, 12).

The Journal’s May 8 report likewise described Rogers as seeing an apparently regular record. It also made clear that he did not know what happened to the slip after Frank took it into the office (AJ, 13).

July 28–29: Newt Lee Repeated His Account at Frank’s Trial

Frank’s trial began on Monday, July 28, 1913. Lee’s examination continued into Tuesday, July 29.

The Brief of Evidence preserves Lee’s account of Frank’s original assessment: “Mr. Frank opened the clock and said the punches were all right, that I hadn't missed any punches” (BOE, 8).

The Journal’s July 29 account recorded Lee’s response to the bloody shirt: “Somebody must have been trying to put it (the murder of Phagan) off on me.” He believed someone had tried to implicate him, but did not identify the planter from personal observation (AJ, 15).

Tuesday, July 29: Detective Starnes Demonstrated That the Clock Could Be Manipulated

Detective John N. Starnes addressed whether the clock record could be manufactured. The Georgian reported a demonstration in which a new watchman produced what appeared to be approximately twelve hours of registrations in about five minutes. The report explained that the state intended to support its contention that “Frank doctored the time tape submitted to the police department” (AG, 16).

The demonstration established that a misleading record could be manufactured quickly. It did not show who, if anyone, had altered Lee’s slip.

Wednesday, July 30: Rogers Repeated His Evidence Before the Jury

The Georgian reported his statement: “There did not appear to be any skip in it.” Its account placed this evidence in the July 30 trial coverage, on page 2, columns 5–6 (AG, 17).

Rogers was one of the prosecution’s strongest witnesses on the initial condition of the slip because he claimed personal observation. Lee could testify about his own rounds and what Frank told him. Rogers could add that he had looked at the record and had not observed the alleged gaps.

Wednesday, July 30: Detective Black Connected Frank to the Changed Explanation

Black was the most direct police witness concerning Frank’s alleged suggestion that Lee had time to leave the factory.

But Black’s chronology was vulnerable. The Georgian quoted him as saying, “He told me Tuesday,” when questioned about the changed account. Lee had placed Frank’s changed statement on Monday morning (AG, 17).

The Constitution’s July 31 report emphasized the difficulties created by Black’s cross-examination. It stated that “Black’s answers failed to bear out the contention of the solicitor” (AC, 18).

The strongest presentation uses Black for what he specifically attributed to Frank, Rogers for the initially regular appearance of the record, and Starnes for the clock’s susceptibility to manipulation.

Thursday, July 31: Harry Scott’s Testimony Complicated the Monday Chronology

Pinkerton detective Harry Scott described a Monday afternoon discussion in which Frank mentioned the first and last clock registrations without drawing attention to the alleged gaps.

The Journal summarized that part of Scott’s evidence: “No discrepancy was remarked by Frank then” (AJ, 7).

Scott’s account complicates the claim that Frank consistently emphasized the gaps throughout Monday. The prosecution had to show that the shifting explanations reflected an attempt to implicate Lee.

Thursday, July 31: The Shirt’s Condition Supported the Planting Argument

Dr. Claude A. Smith’s examination of the bloody shirt gave the prosecution another basis for questioning the evidence against Lee.

Reporting his testimony on August 1, the Journal quoted him: “It had every appearance of having been washed, but not worn.” Smith described features including the condition of the collar, the absence of the expected odor under the arms, and blood staining that raised questions about whether the garment had been worn when stained (AJ, 19).

The observations supported the planting argument without identifying a planter. The defense challenged Smith’s conclusions and the reliability of the indicators he used.

Monday, August 18: Frank Gave His Explanation

In his unsworn statement to the jury, Frank explained that the initial examination had been mistaken. He described looking at the arrangement of the registrations without initially recognizing the missing intervals. He also disputed the implication that his handling of the slip established wrongdoing (Frank, 20).

Saturday, August 23: Dorsey Connected the Slip, the Search, and the Shirt

The Georgian’s August 23 report quoted him saying: “There was not enough evidence against Newt Lee.” Dorsey then argued that the request to search Frank’s residence, associated with Haas, was connected to the suggestion that Lee had time to leave the factory and go home. The relevant passage appears on printed page 3, column 7 (AG, 22).

The Journal’s report, under “The Time Clock Slips” on page 4, column 2, recorded Dorsey’s argument that Frank had suggested “Newt Lee had time to go out to his house and change his clothes.” Dorsey connected that proposition to the subsequent discovery of the shirt (AJ, 23).

Sunday, August 24: The Constitution Published the Argument About Frank’s Changed Figures

Under the subheading “Evidence All Planted,” Dorsey argued that Frank initially described the clock record as accurate, but subsequently changed his position when the shirt required an opportunity for Lee to have visited his residence. The newspaper quoted the accusation that Frank “accordingly changed his figures and altered his statement” (AC, 24).

This was Dorsey’s accusation of changed figures and explanation, not eyewitness testimony that Frank manufactured a replacement slip.

What Can Be Argued About Haas’s Role

Dorsey’s interpretation treated the invitation to search Frank’s residence as a means of encouraging a corresponding search of Lee’s residence. Within that theory, an apparently cooperative request could help direct the investigation toward another suspect (AG, 22; AJ, 23). It was regarded as an intimation, or suggestion by proxy. At the time Leo Frank was not arrested, and Newt Lee was arrested as the prime suspect. 

The Racial Language Surrounding Lee

The newspapers’ descriptions of Lee show the racial attitudes within which his evidence was received.

The Journal’s July 29 profile described him as possessing “the wit and the manner of darkies in old-time slavery days.” That patronizing comparison appeared in its coverage of a Black witness whose liberty had been endangered by the investigation (AJ, 15).

The language shows how even favorable descriptions could place Lee within a sentimentalized image of slavery. He was a working man giving evidence about a murder investigation, yet the newspaper presented his personality through a racial stereotype.

The prosecution’s framing theory therefore has a racial dimension. If Lee was deliberately made to appear guilty, the attempt would have exploited a society already disposed to treat a Black laborer as a convenient suspect. 

The Strongest Historical Argument

Lee said Frank first approved the time record and later criticized it. Rogers said he saw no apparent gaps in the original slip. Black attributed to Frank the suggestion that Lee had sufficient time to travel home. Starnes demonstrated that the clock could produce a misleading record in a matter of minutes if someone had the key to open the clock. Testimony about the shirt’s condition supported the prosecution’s allegation that it had been prepared as incriminating evidence. Dorsey brought those points together in his closing argument.

That is a substantial circumstantial case for examining whether Frank attempted to redirect suspicion toward Lee. It is also an argument with identifiable weaknesses: disputed custody of the slip, inconsistent recollections about timing, an explanation based on an initial misreading, and no cited eyewitness who saw Frank forge the paper or plant the shirt.

Those weaknesses should be assessed against the evidence. They do not erase the evidence or make the historical accusation imaginary.

The Questions Jake Tapper Should Answer

Mr. Tapper, which part of this contemporary record do you contend is ahistorical? Lee’s testimony that Frank initially approved the slip? Rogers’s account of seeing no apparent missing punches? Black’s testimony about the proposed trip home by Frank? The demonstration of the clock’s operation that showed a time slip could be forged if someone had a key to open the clock? Or Dorsey’s published argument connecting the slip, Haas’s request, and the bloody shirt?

A serious response should explain how those records are to be understood. The fact that a prosecution argument was made does not prove it correct. The fact that Frank was Jewish does not place the conduct attributed to him beyond historical examination.

Frank’s subsequent lynching was indefensible. An examination of the allegation that Lee was almost framed for murder by Leo Frank does not justify that killing. It asks whether another man’s vulnerability was exploited during the investigation and whether the surviving evidence supports that charge.

The strongest questions are specific: Who possessed the slip between its initial examination and its later production? Police argued Leo Frank retained Lee's time slip in his custody.

Which witness first identified the time slip on Sunday as punched correctly, but then on Monday stated it was missing intervals? Leo Frank.

When did Frank suggest that Lee had time to travel home? An officer stated Frank said that on Tuesday, but he wasn't sure, it might have been Monday.

What explains the condition of the bloodstained shirt found at Newt Lee’s home on Tuesday, April 29, 1913? Lee had been arrested at 3:30 a.m. on Sunday, April 27, 1913. If the shirt was planted while he was in custody, who put it there, and who had the means, access, and motive to arrange its placement? Could the demand made on Monday, April 28, 1913, to search Leo Frank’s dirty laundry have been intended to prompt a similar search of Lee’s clothing, directing police toward evidence planted to incriminate a man already behind bars?

And how well does the prosecution’s interpretation account for the evidence compared with the explanation Frank offered?

$NVDA closed at $125.79, down 13.84%, a 52-week low and 47.4% below its Oct 6 record close of $239.24. Reuters reported Friday that SEC enforcement staff are examining potential accounting issues at the company, citing two people briefed on the matter. It was down more than 6% before that report crossed.

The business didn't break. Revenue was $115.8 billion last quarter, up 103% from a year ago.

Reuters didn't name the items. The filings offer two. Nvidia books revenue to where customers are headquartered, not where they're billed. And it guarantees its customers' real estate.

Interim CEO Colette Kress said on Tuesday's earnings call that total guarantees were $118 billion, $105 billion of it credit support on one campus. PORTS-Pike in Ohio, 4.25 gigawatts, nine buildings, leased to OpenAI for 20 years. Nvidia pays the shortfall if OpenAI stops paying rent, and those guarantees don't start phasing in until fiscal 2029.

Nobody has alleged Nvidia invented a sale. The guarantee line says something narrower: one tenant, one campus, $105 billion of backstop.

I had Jensen Huang's Nov 12 resignation down as a governance story the stock would digest inside a week. It's down 24% since.

The complex went with it. Micron fell 13.9%, AMD 13.3%, Broadcom 12.2%. The Nasdaq closed 5.3% lower and is now down 2.7% for the year. The 10-year yield fell 14 basis points to 4.91%, so rates aren't it. Gold fell 3.7% to $3,526, its 55th straight close below its own 200-day.

Nvidia's 200-day is at $203.35, 62% above today's close, and this was the 13th straight close under it. If the 10-Q shows guarantees still at $118 billion and the geographic breakdown unchanged, the drop was about governance, not the accounts. If that number grows with revenue, the seller is financing the buyer.

14 STOCKS. EXTRAORDINARY RETURNS. BUT WHICH CAN KEEP COMPOUNDING THROUGH 2030?
Micron +743%. Nebius +248%. Dell +233%.
The past 18 months have produced some remarkable winners. But historical returns tell us very little about what investors can earn from today's valuations.
The bigger question is which companies can sustain earnings growth, defend margins and convert capital investment into free cash flow and attractive returns on invested capital.
STOCK PERFORMANCE | MAY 12, 2025 – NOVEMBER 13, 2026
🔹 $MU Micron: +743.3%
🔹 $NBIS Nebius: +247.5%
🔹 $DELL Dell: +233.2%
🔹 $INTC Intel: +168.9%
🔹 $MRVL Marvell: +143.0%
🔹 $AMAT Applied Materials: +120.5%
🔹 $CRWD CrowdStrike: +111.1%
🔹 $GOOGL Alphabet: +86.6%
🔹 $PANW Palo Alto Networks: +66.5%
🔹 $DDOG Datadog: +62.4%
🔹 $ARM Arm: +52.6%
🔹 $PLTR Palantir: +41.8%
🔹 $HOOD Robinhood: +35.6%
🔹 $NVDA NVIDIA: +32.4%
These are historical share-price returns for the stated period, not forecasts of future performance.
WHAT STANDS OUT TO ME
AI INFRASTRUCTURE CREATED SOME OF THE BIGGEST WINNERS
Micron, Nebius, Dell, Marvell and Applied Materials operate across different parts of the AI buildout: memory, specialised cloud infrastructure, servers, networking/custom silicon and semiconductor manufacturing equipment.
The common driver has been growing demand for AI computing capacity.
But these companies have very different capital requirements, margins, competitive advantages and earnings cycles.
Micron's memory economics are not the same as Nebius's capital-intensive data centre expansion or Marvell's semiconductor design business.
Treating them as interchangeable AI stocks is a mistake.
MICRON SHOWS BOTH THE POWER AND RISK OF THE MEMORY CYCLE
Micron's +743% return is the standout.
AI accelerators require increasingly sophisticated memory, particularly high-bandwidth memory (HBM). Stronger demand and improved pricing have supported earnings growth.
But memory remains cyclical.
Competitors are expanding capacity, and today's favourable supply-demand balance may not persist indefinitely.
I'm bullish on the structural demand for advanced memory, but the investment question is how much of today's profitability can be sustained through the next industry cycle.
A spectacular historical return doesn't eliminate future earnings risk.
NVIDIA'S SMALLER GAIN IS AN IMPORTANT CONTRAST
NVIDIA's +32.4% return looks modest beside Micron, Nebius and Dell.
But that doesn't mean its competitive advantage has weakened.
Starting valuation, investor expectations and sentiment all influence share-price performance.
I remain bullish on NVIDIA's long-term position in accelerated computing, CUDA, networking and integrated AI systems.
However, even the strongest technology platform must justify its valuation through future earnings and cash generation.
I'm also watching hyperscaler custom silicon, gross margins, the Rubin transition and leadership execution.
The company with the strongest technology doesn't automatically deliver the highest future shareholder return.
CYBERSECURITY AND OBSERVABILITY OFFER A DIFFERENT OPPORTUNITY
CrowdStrike, Palo Alto Networks and Datadog have benefited from demand for cloud security, threat protection and infrastructure monitoring.
As AI agents become more deeply integrated into enterprise systems, security, observability and operational reliability could become increasingly important.
But these businesses aren't interchangeable.
CrowdStrike and Palo Alto compete primarily across cybersecurity, while Datadog focuses on observability and cloud monitoring, alongside its security offerings.
I'm watching recurring revenue quality, customer retention, platform adoption, operating margins and free cash flow.
The opportunity is structural, but valuation still determines the attractiveness of future returns.
THE NEXT WINNERS MAY BE VERY DIFFERENT
Not every stock on this list has benefited from the same investment theme.
Alphabet, Palantir, Robinhood and Intel have different business models, competitive challenges and earnings drivers.
A stock up 700% isn't automatically overvalued. A stock up 30% isn't automatically cheap.
What matters is the relationship between future earnings, cash generation, capital requirements and the price investors pay today.
A slower-growing company with strong margins and disciplined capital allocation can outperform a faster-growing business that continually needs debt or equity financing.
That's why I focus on business economics rather than historical share-price performance alone.
MY TAKE
I'm still bullish on the long-term AI investment cycle, particularly across memory, networking, semiconductor equipment, cloud infrastructure and cybersecurity.
But I wouldn't buy any of these companies simply because they've already delivered extraordinary returns.
My investment framework remains:
Capital → Power → Data Centres → Compute → Utilisation → Revenue → Free Cash Flow → ROIC.
Every stage matters.
The AI buildout can create enormous revenue opportunities without necessarily delivering equally attractive shareholder returns.
Backlogs must become recognised revenue. Revenue must translate into margins. Margins must generate cash. And cash returns must justify the capital invested.
WHAT MATTERS NEXT
Through 2030, I expect investors to become increasingly selective about the companies benefiting from AI spending.
The next winners won't necessarily be those announcing the largest contracts, deploying the most GPUs or reporting the fastest revenue growth.
They'll be the companies capable of sustaining competitive advantages, defending profitability and generating attractive returns on capital at valuations that leave room for investors to benefit.
The past 18 months rewarded exposure to powerful growth themes.
The next phase will test the underlying economics.
Which THREE companies on this list offer the strongest risk/reward from today's valuations — and what financial evidence supports your choices?
— EMMANUELINVEST

text:
The United States and Canada are two of the wealthiest countries in North America.

Both offer economic opportunities, developed infrastructure and access to major global industries.

But living in them can mean very different financial trade-offs.

The average American wage is approximately 28% higher when adjusted for purchasing power.

But American workers also spend more hours working each year.

Canada recorded lower inflation in 2025 and fewer average annual working hours.

And here's something worth remembering:

A HIGHER SALARY DOESN'T AUTOMATICALLY MEAN A BETTER STANDARD OF LIVING.

Those wage figures account for purchasing power, but they don't tell you how much money an individual household has left after taxes, housing, healthcare, childcare and transportation.

And fewer working hours don't automatically guarantee a better work-life balance.

The demographic numbers reveal another difference.

Canada's fertility rate was just 1.26 children per woman.

In the United States, it was 1.57.

Both are below the replacement level of approximately 2.1.

So does America's higher average wage automatically make it the better place to live?

Not necessarily.

And does Canada's lower inflation and fewer working hours mean Canadians have an easier life?

Not necessarily either.

Your job, housing costs, family situation and personal priorities can change everything.

Some people would choose the United States for its earning potential and career opportunities.

Others would choose Canada for its lifestyle preferences and public services.

But here's the real question:

If you had to start your life over tomorrow and could choose only ONE country...

WHERE WOULD YOU RATHER LIVE?

🔴 UNITED STATES 🇺🇸

🔵 CANADA 🇨🇦

And if you've actually lived in both, which one would you NEVER move back to?

A letter dated November 20, 2026, from former Salt Lake County Republican Party Chairman Scott Miller to Utah Senate President Stuart Adams.

And it raises some very important questions about what has happened to the Utah Republican Party.

On November 18, President Adams circulated a Deseret News article concerning Josh Kanter, Alliance for a Better Utah, George Soros, and Democratic political funding in Utah.

Adams observed:
“The Republican Party is not united.”
He also stated:
“This article should have been written last April not after the election.”

But it quickly got interesting.
Scott Miller says Republicans were publicly raising these very concerns in AUGUST 2020; SIX YEARS AGO!

Miller included two video scripts dated August 31, 2020, addressing Alliance for a Better Utah, the Kanters, political contributions, and their reported connections to other political organizations.
And what was happening in Salt Lake County in 2020?
REPUBLICANS WERE WINNING!

During Miller's chairmanship, Republican volunteers helped win countywide and district races to secure a supermajority on the Salt Lake County Council, even as Joe Biden carried Salt Lake County by approximately 11 percentage points.

So what happened between 2020 and 2026?

Miller offers part of that history.

Miller describes how he and a party volunteer became the subjects of serious and damaging allegations, most originating from within the Republican Party itself.
Those allegations involved bullying, harassment, sexual harassment, and even sexual assault.

He questions whether the allegations were fairly and thoroughly investigated, what evidence supported them, and what consequences followed for the individuals and volunteers who had contributed to earlier Republican victories.

Now, six years later, Republicans are confronting substantial election losses, with the Salt Lake County Council flipping to a Democratic supermajority and significant Republican losses in the State Legislature.
We must honestly ask what happened INSIDE the Utah Republican Party during those six years.

What happened to the volunteers, leadership, relationships, and organizational knowledge that helped Republicans win elections?
What decisions did Republican leadership make?
What complaints were investigated?
What accountability was provided?
And what lessons have actually been learned?

I have been asking many of these same questions.
I believe Republicans deserve answers supported by facts, documents, and a fair examination of the record.

We cannot rebuild the Utah Republican Party by examining only what Democrats did right. We must also be willing to examine what Utah Republicans did wrong.
I encourage Utah Republican leaders and State Central Committee members to read Scott Miller's November 20 letter and consider the questions he raises.
NO MORE SILENCE.
YOU WILL BE HEARD.

On 𝗡𝗼𝘃𝗲𝗺𝗯𝗲𝗿 𝟮𝟯 (this Monday!), Japan takes a day off for 𝗞𝗶𝗻𝗿𝗼 𝗞𝗮𝗻𝘀𝗵𝗮 𝗻𝗼 𝗛𝗶, or "Labor Thanksgiving Day." Officially, it's a day to respect work, celebrate production, and thank one another.

But its roots go much deeper. It is the modern name for 𝗡𝗶𝗶𝗻𝗮𝗺𝗲𝘀𝗮𝗶 (新嘗祭), an ancient harvest festival in which the Emperor offers the year's 𝗻𝗲𝘄 𝗿𝗶𝗰𝗲 to the gods and tastes it for the first time. Scholars trace its basic form to the late 7th century.

The surprising part: 𝗶𝘁 𝘀𝘁𝗶𝗹𝗹 𝗵𝗮𝗽𝗽𝗲𝗻𝘀. On the night of Nov 23, the Emperor performs the rite at the 𝗦𝗵𝗶𝗻𝗸𝗮𝗱𝗲𝗻 in the Imperial Palace: an evening ceremony from about 6 to 8 PM, then another from 11 PM to 1 AM, offering new rice and sake. 🍶

The date was fixed in 𝟭𝟴𝟳𝟯, when Japan adopted the Western calendar, and in 𝟭𝟵𝟰𝟴, during the postwar occupation, it was renamed as today's secular holiday.

Today, kids make thank-you cards for police officers, firefighters and their parents, while shrines across Japan hold their own Niinamesai with sacred dances. ⛩️

Robert Short just won the job running Wyoming’s elections, promising voters he’d make the secretary of state’s office “boring again.” Weeks later, his first personnel decision is anything but boring — or Republican.

Short tapped Cara Boyle Chambers, a two-decade state government veteran, to serve as his 𝐝𝐞𝐩𝐮𝐭𝐲 𝐬𝐞𝐜𝐫𝐞𝐭𝐚𝐫𝐲 𝐨𝐟 𝐬𝐭𝐚𝐭𝐞, the No. 2 post overseeing how the state runs its elections. Federal Election Commission records show Chambers has sent money to ActBlue, to Joe Biden’s 2020 campaign, and to multiple 2026 Democrat Senate candidates — including Maine’s Graham Platner, the Nazi-tattooed oyster farmer whose campaign collapsed under sexual misconduct allegations.

Confronted with her own donation trail, Chambers didn’t deny a word of it. She just offered Short an out: “𝘐𝘧 𝘐 𝘥𝘰 𝘯𝘰𝘵 𝘤𝘢𝘳𝘳𝘺 𝘰𝘶𝘵 𝘵𝘩𝘦 𝘤𝘰𝘯𝘴𝘵𝘪𝘵𝘶𝘵𝘪𝘰𝘯𝘢𝘭 𝘢𝘯𝘥 𝘴𝘵𝘢𝘵𝘶𝘵𝘰𝘳𝘺 𝘥𝘶𝘵𝘪𝘦𝘴 𝘰𝘧 𝘵𝘩𝘦 𝘰𝘧𝘧𝘪𝘤𝘦, 𝘚𝘖𝘚-𝘦𝘭𝘦𝘤𝘵 𝘚𝘩𝘰𝘳𝘵 𝘤𝘢𝘯 𝘢𝘯𝘥 𝘴𝘩𝘰𝘶𝘭𝘥 𝘵𝘦𝘳𝘮𝘪𝘯𝘢𝘵𝘦 𝘮𝘺 𝘦𝘮𝘱𝘭𝘰𝘺𝘮𝘦𝘯𝘵,” she told Cowboy State Daily — as if bankrolling Biden and ActBlue while running Wyoming’s elections is a problem to fix later, not a decision Short had already made.

Short’s own defense wasn’t any sturdier. He claimed “𝘯𝘰 𝘪𝘥𝘦𝘢” about her donor history, then waved it off anyway as “100% 𝘪𝘳𝘳𝘦𝘭𝘦𝘷𝘢𝘯𝘵 𝘵𝘰 𝘵𝘩𝘦 𝘫𝘰𝘣.” Chambers’ own party registration reportedly read Republican only as recently as September — despite her voting in Wyoming’s Democrat primaries in both 2022 and 2024.

This isn’t a one-off. Short’s own primary campaign ran on an in-kind donation from a Democrat state representative, and the very same week he hired Chambers, incoming GOP Gov. Eric Barlow named a 𝐥𝐢𝐟𝐞𝐥𝐨𝐧𝐠 𝐃𝐞𝐦𝐨𝐜𝐫𝐚𝐭 to be the state’s next attorney general. In deep-red Wyoming, where the Republican primary is effectively the general election, that’s not an accident — it’s the 𝐩𝐥𝐚𝐲𝐛𝐨𝐨𝐤 𝐥𝐢𝐛𝐞𝐫𝐚𝐥𝐬 𝐚𝐫𝐞 𝐫𝐮𝐧𝐧𝐢𝐧𝐠 to control your state from inside the label on your own ballot.

text:
The People Who Weave Themselves Into the Fabric of Our Lives ❤️

Today, after days of rain, the skies finally cleared enough for me to take Toby for a walk around our neighborhood. As I walked past the puddles reflecting the world around me, my thoughts wandered to familiar faces I no longer see. People I didn’t necessarily know personally, yet somehow, over the years, they quietly became part of the fabric of my life.

I thought about Don Ramon, affectionately known as “The Cross Guy,” who faithfully walked our boulevard carrying a large cross on his back. I would honk and wave whenever I passed him, and sometimes stop to offer him water. I understand his health has declined, and I pray he is doing well. Then there was the elderly Asian couple who walked together every morning around 10:30 to feed the ducks at the pond. For years, they were a familiar sight, until one day, there was only her. I often wondered what happened to him.

And I remembered the elderly gentleman who was always outside cutting lawns, greeting me with a smile and a wave as I walked Molly, long before Toby came into my life. Today, I passed the home where he and his wife once lived. The yard was overgrown, the house dark and quiet, and I wondered where life had taken them.

Isn’t it remarkable how people we barely know can leave such lasting impressions on our hearts? We don’t always realize how much their simple presence means until they’re no longer there. As we grow older, perhaps we begin to measure time differently — not just by birthdays and calendars, but by the familiar faces we no longer see, the routines that disappear, and the houses that grow quiet.

Maybe today, I wasn’t simply walking through my neighborhood. I was walking through years of memories. The puddles reflected the world above them, while my heart reflected on the world as it used to be. And it occurred to me that these people may never know they were remembered today, on an ordinary November afternoon, by someone walking her dog.

We may be just a passing face in someone’s day, yet become a lasting memory in their lifetime. ❤️
